questions.prompt: In C++23, is this program well-formed?
options: Well-formed: `a == b` is rewritten as `(a <=> b) == 0`
Ill-formed: `operator<=>` with a deduced return type must be defaulted
questions.explanation: Equality is never rewritten in terms of `<=>`; the rewritten candidates for `==` are only reversed `operator==` functions. An `operator==` is implicitly declared only when `operator<=>` is *defaulted* and no `operator==` is declared, and this one is hand-written. A deduced `auto` return type is fine on a user-written `<=>`.

questions.prompt: In C++20 and later, what does `main` return?
options: Nothing: ill-formed, because `!=` needs a defaulted `operator<=>`
questions.explanation: Since C++20, `a != b` considers the rewritten candidate `!(a == b)`. The defaulted `operator==` compares `x` memberwise, giving false, so `a != b` is true and `main` returns 1. In C++17 this would have been ill-formed, which is the tempting answer; `operator<=>` plays no part in `!=`.

options: Nothing: `<=>` on a NaN is undefined behavior
questions.explanation: Built-in `<=>` on floating-point operands yields `std::partial_ordering`, and when either operand is a NaN the result is `unordered`. An unordered value compares false against literal zero with every relational operator and with `==`, so the first three are 0 and only the comparison with `unordered` is 1. There is no undefined behaviour; partial ordering exists precisely to represent this case.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what happens with this declaration?
options: `r` is `std::strong_ordering::greater`, because `-1` converts to a large unsigned value
questions.explanation: For arithmetic operands, `<=>` applies the usual arithmetic conversions, and [expr.spaceship] makes the program ill-formed if a narrowing conversion is needed, other than integral to floating point. Converting `-1` to `unsigned int` is narrowing. The third option is what `-1 < 1u` effectively does, which is exactly the trap `<=>` was designed to reject.

options: Well-formed: the defaulted `<=>` synthesizes a result from `<` and `==`
Well-formed: `a < b` falls back to `Legacy::operator<` directly
Ill-formed: the defaulted `operator<=>` is defined as deleted, and `a < b` uses it
Ill-formed: a class without `<=>` cannot be a member of a class that defaults `<=>`
questions.explanation: With a deduced `auto` return type, a defaulted `operator<=>` needs `<=>` on every member; `Legacy` has none, so the function is defined as deleted. Declaring the class is fine, but `a < b` selects the deleted function through the rewritten candidate. The fallback to `==` and `<` only happens when the return type is named, such as `std::weak_ordering`, which is why the first option is tempting.

options: `auto`; the type is not fixed until the comparison is evaluated
questions.explanation: A defaulted `operator<=>` with an `auto` return type returns the common comparison category of its member comparisons. `int <=> int` is `std::strong_ordering` and `double <=> double` is `std::partial_ordering`, and the common category is the weakest, `std::partial_ordering`. The first member does not decide the type, even though it is compared first.

questions.prompt: Which of these declarations is ill-formed?
questions.explanation: The comparison category types convert implicitly only towards weaker guarantees: `strong_ordering` to `weak_ordering` and `partial_ordering`, and `weak_ordering` to `partial_ordering`. Turning a weak ordering into a strong one would claim that equivalent values are interchangeable, so no conversion exists. The other three are all permitted widenings.

questions.prompt: Only one comparison function exists. Which expression does the compiler evaluate for `42 < s`, and what is printed?
options: None: the program is ill-formed because `int` has no `operator<=>(S)`
questions.explanation: For `x < y`, [over.match.oper] adds the rewritten candidate `(x <=> y) < 0` and the reversed candidate `0 < (y <=> x)`. Only the reversed form matches the member, so `42 < s` becomes `0 < (s <=> 42)`. Since 5 is less than 42, `s <=> 42` is `less`, and `0 < less` is false, so it prints `member` and `0`. The third option forgets that the reversal also flips which side of zero the result is tested on.
